title: Have you ever had the mulligrubs? | LOST WORDS

entries.note: A 14th-century word meaning 'it seems to me', used much like [[see:methinks]]; one of the useful antiquated words the hosts want to revive.
The model for [[see:meseems]]; the hosts joke that someone saying methinks is not normally a good sign.
Used from Middle English into the 17th century to mean soon afterwards, as in 'I'll see you eftsoons'.
An old time-frame word for a year, which the hosts say makes perfect sense.
The Old English word for an hour before the French import [[see:hour]] arrived; related Germanic words include German [[same-root:Stunde]].
The German word for an hour, cited as a Germanic relative of Old English [[same-root:stound]].
A French import that replaced Old English [[see:stound]]; also linked to the clockmaker's word [[same-root:horologer]].
In Britain it once meant a million million rather than today's thousand million; the old word for a thousand million was [[see:milliard]].
The old British word for a thousand million, which Jess says sounds like a million mallard ducks.
Means 10,000; after viewers objected to 'a myriad of', the hosts point out that both the noun and adjective uses have been legitimate since the 16th–17th centuries.
The Old English name for February, meaning mud month.
The Old English name for March, which the hosts say meant a quick month, or a month of nimbleness and activity.
The Old English name for April, Easter month, which Rob says makes sense.
An Old English month name, probably May, said to come from cows being so fertile that they could be milked three times a day.
The Old English name for November, when early Saxons prepared for winter by sacrificing animals, then butchering and storing them for food.
An old word for Friday evening, the eve of Saturday.
A 13th-century word for dawn, which reminds Jess of the video game [[see:Skyrim]].
Jess's favourite video game, brought to mind by [[see:dayrim]]; it has a lot of Old Norse influence in its character and place names.
An obsolete word for the day of one's death, with a fairly transparent meaning.
A 14th-century word for a clockmaker, from the same source as [[same-root:hour]].
An old word for a timepiece, sundial or hourglass, comparable to French [[same-root:horloge]].
The French word for a clock or timepiece, which Rob compares with [[same-root:horologe]].
A French job title that originally meant someone who made carriages and carts; the Old English term was [[equivalent:treewright]].
From French, originally someone who dealt only in goat meat, from [[from:buck]], a male goat; related to [[same-root:springbok]]. It replaced Old English [[see:fleshmonger]].
The old word for a [[see:butcher]] before English took that word from French.
Cited as related to [[same-root:butcher]] through buck, a male goat.
Someone who habitually made money from spurious lawsuits, roughly what we might now call an [[see:ambulance chaser]].
A nasty old nickname for a doctor, from the practice of judging health by examining urine; the hosts compare it with [[see:humorism]].
Discussed in an earlier episode of the podcast.
An old term for a pimp.
The Old English term for a [[equivalent:carpenter]], which Jess says makes more literal sense than the French word.
A word for a maker found in many old job titles, often used figuratively, as in poemwright; related to [[same-root:wrought]].
An old word for a baker, one of the many [[see:wright]] job titles.
An old word for a soldier, one of the [[see:wright]] job titles.
An old word for a builder, one of the [[see:wright]] job titles.
A poet, given as an example of the figurative use of [[see:wright]].
Rob's favourite [[see:wright]], a maker of puddings in the old savoury sense, though he likes to imagine sponge cakes.
Cited as related to [[same-root:wright]].
An alternative word for a maker of carts and carriages, the original sense of [[see:carpenter]], which now survives mainly as a surname.
An old word for a midwife, also a nickname for a pickpocket.
A very old word: mid meant with and wife originally meant woman, so it was the person with the woman, not necessarily a woman herself.
Fairly modern US slang for someone who talks too much, quoted from the Philadelphia Saturday Evening Post in 1910.
A Latin-derived coinage from [[from:ventus]], wind, recorded from the 14th to 19th centuries, meaning either flatulence or being a windbag; often used by [[see:Washington Irving]].
Used [[see:ventosity]] frequently in his works about New York culture, such as Salmagundi and his history of New York, which contain fun coinages.
Originally a woman who spun thread for a living, with the feminine [[see:-ster]] ending; it came to mean unmarried women because they traditionally took up spinning.
An agent-noun ending, now gender-neutral as in [[see:trickster]] and [[see:gangster]], but feminine in Middle English, unlike -er.
An example of the now gender-neutral [[see:-ster]] ending.
An example of the now gender-neutral [[see:-ster]] ending.
An example of the gender-neutral or masculine -er ending, in contrast to [[see:-ster]].
An example of the gender-neutral or masculine -er ending, in contrast to [[see:-ster]].
An example of the gender-neutral or masculine -er ending, in contrast to [[see:-ster]].
A woman who sewed for a living, used before [[see:seamstress]] arrived with its French -ess ending.
Its French -ess ending replaced the older feminine [[see:-ster]] of [[see:sewster]].
A woman who bleached cloth, with the feminine [[see:-ster]] ending.
A surname originally meaning a woman weaver, with the feminine [[see:-ster]] ending.
A surname originally meaning a woman brewer; a female brewer Rob interviewed insisted on being called a brewster.
From bakester, a woman baker; a change in spelling hides it in plain sight, and it is a family name on one side of Jess's family.
One of Rob's favourite old names for a spider, essentially a web spinner using an old form of the verb.
An old word for a spider, similar to the French [[same-root:araignée]] and from the same Latin root.
The French for spider, compared with English [[same-root:arain]].
An old word for a spider, literally venom head, related to [[same-root:cobweb]] and used in a song in [[see:The Hobbit]]; unrelated to [[unrelated:adder]].
Simply a spider web, from [[from:cop]], and related to [[same-root:attercop]].
An old word for a spider, found in [[gave:cobweb]].
The dwarves sing a song using [[see:attercop]] to anger the spiders in Mirkwood; Jess has a tattoo from Tolkien's own drawing of Smaug in the 1955 edition.
An old job title for a swordmaker, from [[from:bilbo]], a type of sword; a [[see:The Hobbit]] reference.
Not related to [[unrelated:attercop]], because the word should be nadder.
An old word for a spider, a little walking weaver, from [[from:gang]], an old word for walk.
An old word for a rabbit, which may have given [[gave:Coney Island]] its name.
Perhaps named after its rabbit population, from [[from?:coney]], or after somewhere else that took its name from rabbits.
An old word for a [[see:porpoise]], used before people called them porpoises.
Means pig fish; the hosts correct an earlier error, reading a dictionary definition of a [[see:delphinid]] whale with a blunt snout, but still aren't sure how it relates to [[see:dolphin]]s.
In an earlier episode the hosts wrongly said a dolphin is a type of [[see:porpoise]], and they still aren't sure of the relationship.
Used to define [[see:porpoise]]; the hosts wonder whether it means dolphin-like or dolphin-shaped, and so whether it includes dolphins.
From French, originally Greek for shadow tail and related to [[same-root:obscure]]; it replaced Old English [[see:acweorna]] and is supposedly English's longest one-syllable word.
Thought to be related to [[same-root:squirrel]], through the idea of shadow.
The old English word for a [[see:squirrel]]; its first part means oak, and the whole is best guessed to mean oak dweller.
The German word for a squirrel, which Rob thinks shows some folk etymology because it means roughly little acorn; it is related to the oak, like Old English [[see:acweorna]].
An old name for the giraffe, literally camel leopard; it is also a southern hemisphere constellation that could have featured in their space episode.
Comes from Arabic [[from:zarafa]]; older Middle English names include [[see:camelopard]], [[see:gerfaunt]] and [[see:orafle]].
A brief Middle English name for a giraffe, whose ending was influenced by the -fant of [[see:elephant]], used for exotic animals.
Its -fant ending influenced the giraffe name [[see:gerfaunt]].
An old name for a giraffe, probably from the Latin version of Arabic [[from:zarafa]].
A word for anything with one horn, either a [[see:rhinoceros]] or a [[see:unicorn]] depending on context; it appears in Herbert Coleridge's dictionary.
One of the animals [[see:monoceros]] could refer to; Jess suggests calling one-horned rhinoceroses monoceroses.
The other meaning of [[see:monoceros]]; Rob jokes that a one-horned rhino is a heavy unicorn.
A synonym for openly from Coleridge's dictionary, comparable to [[same-root:aperture]].
An opening, cited to explain [[same-root:apertly]].
Meaning confused or perplexed; Rob covered it in one of his videos, and a relative survives in northern English dialect as [[same-root:mither]].
A northern English dialect relative of [[same-root:bemazed]]: someone who really bothers you is mithering you.
A prefix popular in the 15th and 16th centuries, most often meaning around or on all sides, as in [[see:besiege]], but also privative, as in [[see:behead]].
To thrash someone very soundly; one of the [[see:be-]] words Jess wants to bring back.
To give someone a verbal thrashing, another word formed with [[see:be-]].
To make a fool of someone; a [[see:be-]] word that still comes up a little today.
An example of [[see:be-]] meaning around or on all sides.
An example of [[see:be-]] meaning around or on all sides.
An example of the privative use of [[see:be-]], meaning depriving of something.
To insult someone by making them the object of mirth, although it sounds like filling them with too much joy.
Describes doing something of your own accord without real cause; it made Rob snort and blush.
To displease someone.
Meant pregnant; the etymology is uncertain, but Rob thinks it is probably related to [[from?:blossom]].
To give birth to a child, or bring one forth.
Recorded in Francis Grose's 1785 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue: a man whose scrotum hangs lower than his penis; supposedly related to [[same-root?:rantipole]].
Referred to a sexual position with the woman on top, facing the other way; supposedly related to [[same-root?:rantallion]].
Having beautiful buttocks, named after the [[from:Callipygian Venus]] statue of Aphrodite.
A statue of Aphrodite whose lost head was supposedly reattached so she looks back over her shoulder at her shapely buttocks; it gave [[gave:callipygian]].
A Francis Grose word for a little white lie.
One of the old fanciful words for a liar: someone who specialised in falsehoods.
An old word for a liar, someone who adds figurative wrinkles to the truth.
An old word for a liar, which Jess says makes sense.
An old word for a liar that Jess doesn't fully understand yet; she learned it from the card game League of the Lexicon.
An old word for a liar that Jess hasn't fully researched yet.
An old word for a liar that Jess hasn't fully researched yet.
Someone who stubbornly insists they are right; popularised by [[see:Erasmus]]'s story of a priest who kept saying mumpsimus for [[from:quod ore sumpsimus]].

entries.translation: what we have received by the mouth
entries.note: Words from the communion service that a priest kept mispronouncing, which gave [[gave:mumpsimus]].
An old word for a scarecrow from Coleridge's dictionary, which reminds Rob of [[see:emmet]].
A term used in south-west England to insult tourists, people not from the area.
A medieval word for a stranger, meaning someone who has come; one of the many old [[see:-ling]] words.
The hosts discussed -ling words in an earlier episode.
A fit of the blues, or sometimes a vague abdominal pain; its exact origin is unknown.
Describes someone who snores a lot.
Belching; Rob recalls a dictionary describing it as a gassy, meaty emission.
A rare word meaning to spit on, probably a fanciful Latinate form like [[same-root:sputum]], from Latin [[from:spuere]]; used in the Saturday Review about the Shakespeare–Bacon craze.
Cited as coming from the same Latin source as [[same-root:conspue]].
From Latin [[from:jacere]], to throw; it means swaggering or swaying, so boasting or thrashing in one's sleep, and sounds naughtier than it is.
Sounds like [[see:jactitation]]; it now has an almost solely crude meaning but used to mean simply to exclaim.
One of the words for a commotion still used today, alongside older words like [[see:hubble-shubble]].
One of the words for a commotion still used today.
One of the words for a commotion still used today.
One of the old imitative or onomatopoeic words for the actions and sounds of fighting.
An old imitative or onomatopoeic word for the actions and sounds of fighting.
An old imitative or onomatopoeic word for the actions and sounds of fighting.
A Middle English word meaning to dance gracelessly, without much art or skill but perhaps with some enjoyment; one of Jess's two words to revive.
To hide yourself in a corner; Jess's other word to revive, for when you don't feel like [[see:balter]]ing.
Rob thought it was rare and put it in his newsletter, but it is widely known in the US, with many spellings such as caddywampus.
